q: A young Muscadet reaches the table with a faint prickle on the tongue and a bready, creamy edge. What accounts for both at once?
opts: A second fermentation carried out in the bottle
Bottling the wine straight off its own fine lees
Malolactic conversion completed in new oak barrels
A small dosage of sugar syrup added before bottling
exp: Nothing is added and nothing ferments twice. Carbon dioxide left over from the original fermentation stays dissolved because the wine is never racked, and the spent yeast contributes the texture.

q: Two small rivers south-east of Nantes lend their names to the most important of the Muscadet appellations. Which is it?
exp: The Sevre Nantaise and the Maine drain the heart of the vineyard. Coteaux de la Loire and Cotes de Grandlieu are the other two named zones, and Coteaux d'Ancenis is a separate appellation entirely.

q: A bottle of Clisson has rested on its lees far longer than a standard Muscadet, yet the words sur lie appear nowhere on the label. Why are they absent?
opts: The wine was raised in barrel rather than in tank
Sur lie may only be used on the generic Muscadet appellation
The cru rules require lees ageing beyond the sur lie limit
The wine was racked off its lees immediately after fermentation
exp: Sur lie is tied to an early bottling, in the year after the harvest. The cru communal rules demand lees ageing well beyond that: Clisson keeps its wine on lees for two years at least. The crus gain concentration and texture but forfeit the term that made the region's name.

q: A plate of raw oysters arrives and the sommelier reaches for the Atlantic end of the valley. Which qualities make that match work?
opts: Low alcohol, high acidity and a dry, unoaked finish
Noticeable residual sugar over an oak-aged texture
Botrytis character carried on low acidity
Firm tannin supported by high alcohol
exp: Acidity does the work a squeeze of lemon would, and the absence of oak or sweetness leaves the shellfish untouched. Low alcohol keeps the wine from flattening something as delicate as a raw oyster, and Muscadet's own faint salinity meets the brine halfway. It is the closest thing the wine list has to a default pairing.

q: A second white appellation around Nantes works with Folle Blanche and is leaner and sharper still than its famous neighbour. What is it called?
exp: Folle Blanche is so high in acid that it was long grown mainly for distillation into brandy. As a table wine it is austere, cheap and very good with the same shellfish.

q: Steep dark schist slopes on the north bank downstream of Angers give France's most austere and long-lived dry Chenin. Which appellation?
exp: Poor rock, low yields and full southern exposure make a wine that can be almost forbidding in youth. Ten years usually turns the austerity into honey, quince and wet wool.

q: One Savennieres vineyard was granted an appellation in its own name and sits as a single walled amphitheatre of vines above the river. Which is it?
exp: Coulee de Serrant and Roche aux Moines are the two named crus carved out of Savennieres. Clos du Papillon is a celebrated lieu-dit but not an appellation of its own.

q: Rose de Loire, Rose d'Anjou and Cabernet d'Anjou all cover pink wine from the same corner of the valley. Which of the three must be finished dry?
opts: Both Rose d'Anjou and Cabernet d'Anjou
exp: Rose de Loire is the dry one by law. Rose d'Anjou is off-dry and built on Grolleau, while Cabernet d'Anjou is medium sweet and made only from the two Cabernets.

q: Which variety dominates the reds of Anjou-Villages and gives them their leafy, raspberry-scented profile?
exp: Anjou-Villages is the stricter red appellation sitting above plain Anjou Rouge, with lower yields and later release. Cabernet Franc carries it, as it carries almost every serious Loire red.

q: Loire growers have long used a local name for Chenin Blanc that misleads visitors into thinking of Burgundy. What is it?
exp: Pineau de la Loire has nothing to do with Pinot. Chenin's real home is here, and outside the valley only South Africa, where it was long called Steen, grows it in quantity.

q: Soft white limestone quarried for the chateaux of the valley left miles of galleries beneath the town of Saumur. What is that rock called?
exp: Tuffeau is a porous, sandy chalk laid down in a warm Cretaceous sea. It cuts easily when freshly quarried and hardens in the air, which is why so much of the region is built and cellared in it.

q: A cool, humid cellar cut into rock and holding a steady temperature all year suits one wine style above all. Which became the speciality of Saumur?
exp: Bottle-fermented wine needs cool, stable storage in bulk for months or years, and the quarries provided exactly that for nothing. The trade grew up around the cellars rather than the vineyards.

q: A red grown on the limestone plateau immediately east of Saumur is the most sought-after Cabernet Franc of Anjou-Saumur. Which appellation?
exp: The shallow soil over tuffeau warms quickly and drains hard, ripening Cabernet Franc more fully than the surrounding zone. The wines are supple and perfumed, and the best of them age well.

q: One Loire sparkling appellation may draw grapes from Anjou, Saumur and Touraine alike, and requires hand harvesting and whole-bunch pressing. Which is it?
exp: Cremant de Loire is the valley-wide appellation with the tighter rulebook: compulsory hand picking into crates, whole-bunch pressing and a press yield capped at 100 litres of must per 150 kilos of fruit. Those are its genuine extra demands rather than the lees minimum, which Vouvray Mousseux matches.

q: Piercing acidity and orchard-fruit character make one variety the natural base for Loire sparkling wine. Which grape?
exp: Chenin holds acidity at ripeness better than almost any white grape, which is what a base wine needs. Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc and Pinot Noir play supporting roles in the blends.

q: Pressing intact bunches rather than crushed fruit is compulsory for Cremant. What does the rule protect?
opts: Deeper colour drawn from the skins
Clean, pale juice with few phenolics
A higher sugar concentration in the must
A faster and warmer first fermentation
exp: Whole bunches form their own drainage bed, so the press works gently and the juice runs clear. Broken black berries would bleed colour and hard phenolics into a wine meant to be delicate.
